extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, applicants, and academics studying inventive_step/obviousness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing inventive step (obviousness) for patent applications, primarily in the EPO/TBA context: tests, evidentiary indicia, the role and proper use of the problem–solution approach, and how to treat hindsight, common general knowledge and secondary indications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success vs. mere hope
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination seems to have been obvious to try and there was no reasonable expectation of success the invention might involve an inventive step. A reasonable expectation of success should not be confused with the understandable hope to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous work by others may suggest it was "obvious to try" or an "interesting area to explore" but does not necessarily imply a reasonable expectation of success. Examiners should distinguish between mere hope/interest and a rational expectation grounded in the prior art or common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicia (objective evidence supporting inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary indications may be investigated when the objective evaluation of prior art does not give a clear picture; they are no substitute for the technically skilled assessment of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of secondary indicia: long-felt but unsolved need (inactive state of the art with an urgent need for improvement); immediate commercial success that is derived from the features of the invention and coupled with evidence of a long-felt want. Commercial success must be tied to the invention's technical features and not explained by selling techniques or advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution approach is optional (not sine qua non)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem–solution approach is "no more than one possible route for the assessment of inventiveness" and is derived from Rule 42(1)(c) EPC (concerned with description rather than inventiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages and drawbacks exist: the approach was developed to ensure objectivity and to avoid hindsight, but it relies on searches made with knowledge of the invention and thus can be inherently based on hindsight. It is therefore one method among others and not mandatory; examiners may use alternative methods provided they avoid hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest prior art not always required — reasonable selection suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to determine the single "closest prior art" when there is a reasonable selection of prior art; being tied to a particular closest document may prevent consideration of other reasonable lines of attack or defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable selection of prior art can be used as the starting point for the objective formulation of the problem; examiners should not be constrained by selecting a single closest prior art if other documents reasonably form part of the selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight / ex-post facto analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct use of the problem–solution approach rules out an ex-post facto analysis which inadmissibly makes use of knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must take care not to formulate artificial technical problems or to use the invention's disclosure in a way that imports hindsight. Special caution where the same person both formulates the problem and assesses inventive step. Arguments that rely on ex-post interpretation of documents should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness depends on whether prior art points to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of inventiveness depends on whether there is any pointer in the prior art which points to the invention or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art 'clearly points away' from obtaining the claimed invention, then even if a PSA following prior art instructions arrived at the invention, that does not necessarily make it obvious. Conversely, absence of any teaching/pointer towards the technical measure weighs in favour of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of the Person Skilled in the Art (PSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSA must be clearly outlined before assessment; GE characterises PSA as expert in the technical field but not possessed of any inventive or creative capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should specify the level and content of common general knowledge attributed to the PSA. Decisions often fail to discuss PSA skills or general knowledge thoroughly — examiners should be explicit about what PSA would know and be able to do (including routine experiments) without attributing inventive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge and routine experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Common general knowledge for the PSA should be investigated and emphasised; PSA is expected to do necessary experiments to improve a product but not to possess inventive creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish routine, expectable experiments (which PSA may carry out with a reasonable expectation of success) from inventive experimental sequences. Lack of documentary evidence of common general knowledge weakens arguments that PSA would have been led to the claimed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergistic technical effects of combined features
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of known features that interact synergistically to achieve a technical effect (e.g., transistors interconnected to form a microprocessor) may be non-obvious compared with their individual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating combinations, assess whether the combined features produce a new technical effect or synergy not suggested by the prior art; mere aggregation of known features without synergistic effect is less likely to be inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for treating prior art teachings as motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: TBA decisions show that absence in the prior art of a teaching towards a technical measure and absence of documentary evidence in support of common general knowledge do not support that PSA would have considered that technical measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should require an explicit hint, teaching, or documentary support that would motivate the PSA to modify the prior art in the claimed manner; mere availability of different types of solutions in other fields is insufficient without a demonstrated link or motivation.
